title: Revealing names of Hells Angels a death sentence: gang expert: Author of book on biker gangs calls shooting on 401 'highly unusual'
article: A biker gang expert says anyone involved in a shootout with OPP is as good as dead if he gives up names of his alleged Hells Angels contacts.

Yves Lavigne, author of four books on organized crime -- three dealing with the Hells Angels -- says until OPP turn up enough evidence to charge an accused with something more serious, he has a stronger incentive not to co-operate with police.

"If he rats out, he's a dead man. He can name the Hell's Angels he works for, and they can be arrested and prosecuted." Referring to the shootout on the 401 Sunday, Mr. Lavigne said "for now, they haven't got much on him."
Mr. Lavigne, who writes from a private location because of previous attempts made on his life, added: "For most bikers, doing jail time is part of doing business."
Marc Bouffard, 27, was driving a red Pontiac Sunfire that was pulled over by Ontario Provincial Police Const. Dan Brisson on Sunday morning, allegedly for speeding on Highway 401.
Const. Brisson was shot by Mr. Bouffard's associate, Daniel Lamer, 37, of Montreal.
Mr. Lamer was then shot and killed by OPP officers at the scene. Mr. Bouffard, a former member of the Rockers biker gang, was allegedly in the process of being recruited into the Quebec Hells Angels.
He was charged Sunday with attempting to escape police, and for impersonating a man named Eric Martin. More charges are expected.
Mr. Lavigne called the incident Sunday "highly unusual.
"Bikers do not shoot cops -- it causes way too many problems for them," he said. "You shoot a cop, you've got thousands of cops going after you."
The Montreal native testified last Nov. 28 before a Senate committee reviewing the federal government's much-touted organized crime bill, C-24, which has since become law.

A police raid leading to the arrest yesterday of 17 members of a Hells Angels affiliate gang was not evidence of a wider police crackdown on biker gangs, Mr. Lavigne said, though it may have been a convenient publicity stunt.
"If there's a crackdown, this has been in the works for months. But everyone knows a police shooting gets more attention, so obviously this is an attempt to get more attention."
In his 1999 expose Hells Angels at War, Mr. Lavigne wrote that top police officials had conspired to use the public's fear of bikers to boost their departmental budgets.

"The police deliberately misled and scared the public, then extended their caps for money, he said. "They never intended to stop the spread of the Hells Angels from coast to coast and now we're paying for that," he said.
Sgt. Richard Bourdon, whose anti-biker brigade yesterday arrested six members of the Satan Guards, from the Saguenay region north of Quebec City, said the timing of the raid was pure coincidence.
"When the Crown decides you have enough evidence, you make the arrest. This was a one-and-a-half year operation. We got the go- ahead last month."
